title: Swiss and Savoy Witch Trials: Earliest Mass Prosecutions
description:
The Swiss and Savoy regions witnessed some of the earliest well-documented mass witch prosecutions in European history during the mid-fifteenth century, representing a crucial transitional moment when the theoretical construction of the cumulative concept of witchcraft moved into judicial practice. These trials, concentrated in the Alpine regions, systematically combined elements that had previously existed separately in law and theology: the maleficium (harmful magic), the diabolical pact, flight to nocturnal assemblies, and participation in the sabbath. The prosecutions drew on the theoretical groundwork laid by earlier inquisitors and jurists, particularly in the Dauphiné and Savoy, where secular and ecclesiastical courts cooperated in unprecedented ways to pursue what they understood as an organized heretical sect.

The Swiss trials of this period are particularly significant because they produced detailed confessional records describing sabbath activities that would become standardized across European demonological literature. Accused witches described flight to mountain gatherings, feasts, dancing, and sexual intercourse with demons — elements that appeared in Nider's Formicarius (1435) and would be systematized in the Malleus Maleficarum three decades later. The Alpine geography, with its isolated communities and strong beliefs in mountain spirits and nocturnal gatherings, appears to have provided fertile ground for the fusion of learned demonological theory with local folk practice.

Historians have debated the extent to which these early prosecutions represent a genuine cumulation of pre-existing beliefs versus an imposition of elite theological frameworks onto popular practice. Richard Kieckhefer's analysis emphasizes how the cumulative concept of witchcraft — the idea that maleficent magic necessarily implied diabolical pact and sabbath attendance — was constructed through a series of intellectual steps between roughly 1370 and 1450, with the Swiss trials representing its first systematic judicial application.
historiographical_note: Richard Kieckhefer's concept of 'cumulative witchcraft' is directly demonstrated by these early Swiss and Savoy trials. Norman Cohn in Europe's Inner Demons (1975) traced the intellectual genealogy of the sabbath concept and found these Alpine prosecutions central to its development. Stuart Clark notes how these trials show the cumulative concept migrating from theological treatise to judicial practice, while Peter Maxwell-Stuart's survey of witch trials treats the Swiss cases as the foundational model for later European mass prosecutions.
source_method: Published scholarship on early witch trials; trial records via Kieckhefer, Cohn, and Blauert's archival research
